summary:
Guerrero stands under Mexico's national framework on legal gender recognition, and that framework is the only documented layer for this record. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that recognition is set state by state: 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated an administrative procedure, two more operated one in practice without enactment, six state legislatures had enacted nothing, and only seven states extended recognition to children.

Two higher authorities constrain what the states may do. Mexico's Supreme Court set binding guidelines for the states in 2022 and extended the right to minors in the same year, and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights requires a simple, accessible procedure. Where a state has not enacted its own procedure, this national framework governs the visitor's expectations.

Human Rights Watch documents the practical consequence of an absent procedure: identity-document mismatch drives discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, with incidents recorded in Guanajuato and Tabasco. Neither of those states is Guerrero, and no Guerrero-specific statute, court ruling or incident record is supported by the vetted sources.

The Human Rights Watch and Community Center for Inclusion report of 6 March 2024, examining a Mexican state with no recognition procedure, found that without identity documents matching a trans person's gender, every document request and every appearance under scrutiny carries risk of violence, harassment and humiliation. Trans people are excluded from employment, health services, education and financial transactions as a result. The report's context includes the August 2023 murder of trans woman Karina Gomez in Villahermosa and the finding that more than 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022.

For a trans visitor, the practical read is that entry into Guerrero means relying on a patchwork: documents issued in a state with a procedure travel with the holder, while local administrative capacity in Guerrero itself is not documented here.
tangentialFactors:
Violence against trans people in Mexico is documented at national scale rather than in Guerrero. AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City; Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100.

Legislatures have begun to close specific gaps. Mexico City's Congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide; the statute takes its name from a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities in 2024 to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice; the analysis cautions that its earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

Partnership recognition is settled at national level: same-sex marriage has been legal in Mexico since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction.
localsOnly:
Residents of Guerrero rely on the national recognition framework where no local procedure is enacted, meaning the administrative route to a name and gender marker runs through mechanisms set by Mexico's Supreme Court, whose 2022 guidelines bind the states and extend the right to minors. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights requirement of a simple, accessible procedure applies alongside them.

For residents, the documented lived effect of document mismatch in states without a procedure is exclusion from employment, health services, education and financial transactions, together with harassment at every document request. Reported incidents of this kind sit in Guanajuato and Tabasco, not Guerrero.

Impunity shapes daily risk: more than 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022, and the Inter-American Commission warned in 2024 that impunity for violence against LGBTI people may have reached alarming levels. Trans women have been killed in documented cases including Karina Gomez in Villahermosa in August 2023 and activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca in Mexico City in January 2024.

Residents married to a partner of the same sex have been able to do so nationwide since 2009.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Guerrero's legislature has enacted an administrative legal gender-recognition procedure, and whether one operates there in practice without enactment, is not resolved by the vetted sources; the counts of 22 enacted, two practiced and six without any are national tallies that do not attribute a status to Guerrero.

No Guerrero-specific court ruling, administrative directive, police practice, hate-crime provision or documented incident of violence against a trans person appears in the inventory, so local enforcement conditions remain unsourced rather than absent.

Guerrero's position on recognition for children, and whether the Supreme Court's 2022 extension to minors has been applied there in practice, is likewise not documented here.
